05. Getting Started with NNS: Sampling and Simulation

Fred Viole

Source: vignettes/NNSvignette_05_Sampling.Rmd
NNSvignette_05_Sampling.Rmd
library(NNS)
require(knitr)
require(rgl)

NNS offers several novel sampling methods from any distribution, as well as simulating variables while maintaining their dependence.

Sampling

CDFs

Cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) represent the probability a variable XX will take a value less than or equal to xx. F(x)=P(X≤x)F(x) = P(X \leq x)

Empirical CDF

The empirical CDF is a simple construct, provided in the base package of R. We can generate an empirical CDF with the ecdf function and create a function (P) to return the CDF of a given value of XX.

set.seed(123); x = rnorm(100)
ecdf(x)
## Empirical CDF 
## Call: ecdf(x)
##  x[1:100] = -2.3092, -1.9666, -1.6867,  ...,  2.169, 2.1873
P = ecdf(x)
P(0); P(1)
## [1] 0.48
## [1] 0.83

Lower Partial Moment CDF (LPM.ratio)

The empirical CDF and Lower Partial Moment CDF (LPM.ratio) are identical when the degree term of the LPM.ratio is set to zero.

Degree 0 LPM: LPM(0,t,X)=1N∑n=1N[max(t−Xn),0]0LPM(0,t,X)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}[max(t-X_n),0]^0LPM.ratio is equivalent to the following form for any target (t)(t) and variable XX: LPM(0,t,X)=LPM(0,t,X)LPM(0,t,X)+UPM(0,t,X)LPM(0,t,X)=\frac{LPM(0,t,X)}{LPM(0,t,X)+UPM(0,t,X)}

Using the same targets from our ecdf example above (0,1) we can compare LPM.ratios.

LPM.ratio(degree = 0, target = 0, variable = x); LPM.ratio(degree = 0, target = 1, variable = x)
## [1] 0.48
## [1] 0.83

Calculating the probability for every target value in XX, we can plot both methods visualizing their identical results. ecdf function in black and LPM.ratio in red.

LPM.ratio degree > 0

Increasing degree changes the target from event frequency to a directional severity share. In the univariate case with the required finite moment and nondegeneracy, this defines an induced CDF whose law generally differs from the original empirical law. It is not a smoothing operation that automatically preserves original probabilities.

Generating PDFs with (LPM.VaR)

The corresponding LPM.VaR inverts the selected directional curve. Degree zero uses R type-7 empirical quantiles; degree one gives expectiles. Drawing uniforms and applying a positive-degree inverse samples the induced law, not the original marginal law.

The general form in the following plots is:

LPM.VaR(percentile = seq(0, 1, length.out = 100), degree = 0, x = x)

Any length percentile can be used to sample from the underlying distribution xx.

Viewing the first 10 samples from each of the degrees compared to our original XX.

degree.0.samples = LPM.VaR(percentile = seq(0, 1, length.out = 100), degree = 0, x = x)
degree.0.25.samples = LPM.VaR(percentile = seq(0, 1, length.out = 100), degree = 0.25, x = x)
degree.0.5.samples = LPM.VaR(percentile = seq(0, 1, length.out = 100), degree = 0.5, x = x)
degree.1.samples = LPM.VaR(percentile = seq(0, 1, length.out = 100), degree = 1, x = x)
degree.2.samples = LPM.VaR(percentile = seq(0, 1, length.out = 100), degree = 2, x = x)

head(data.frame(check.names = FALSE, cbind("original x" = sort(x), degree.0.samples, 
                                                          degree.0.25.samples, 
                                                          degree.0.5.samples, 
                                                          degree.1.samples, 
                                                          degree.2.samples)), 10)

Simulation

Bootstrapping (NNS.meboot)

NNS.meboot is based on the maximum entropy bootstrap, available in the R-package meboot. Its rank-based scenario construction is useful for time-series exploration. The default force.clt constrains replicate means using an iid standard-error scale, so preserving rank structure does not by itself provide calibrated sampling uncertainty for serial dependence.

Specified rank-correlation targets explore a chosen range of scenario shapes. They do not enumerate every possible future path. A zero rank-correlation target does not imply independence, and achieved marginal distributions and moments must be checked for the chosen settings.

We will generate 1 replicate of XX for each value of a sequence of ρ\rho values (the ensembleensemble), and then plot the results compared to our original XX (black line). NNS.MC is a streamlined wrapper function for this functionality of NNS.meboot.

set.seed(123)
boots = NNS.MC(x, reps = 1, lower_rho = -1, upper_rho = 1, by = .5)$replicates
reps = do.call(cbind, boots)


matplot(reps, type = "l", col = rainbow(length(boots)))
lines(x, type = "l", lwd = 3, ylim = c(min(reps), max(reps)))

Checking our replicate correlations:

sapply(boots, function(r) cor(r, x, method = "spearman"))

#>     rho = 1   rho = 0.5     rho = 0  rho = -0.5    rho = -1
#>  0.99840384  0.50357036  0.01478548 -0.46829883 -0.97912991

More replicates and ensembles thereof can be generated for any number of ρ\rho values.

Note — where the ρ\rho target lives. The dependence alignment is applied to each replicate individually and in residual space: each replicate’s residuals are mixed between the aligned and anti-aligned orderings of the original residuals so that their dependence matches the requested ρ\rho (book Chapter 20). For a series without trend, as here, that is also the dependence on the series itself, which the per-replicate correlations above confirm. For a trending series the replicates keep the trend, so their correlation with the original series can stay high even at ρ=−1\rho = -1: on AirPassengers, ρ=−1\rho = -1 replicates have a mean Spearman correlation of about 0.8 with the series. Two things to keep in mind when checking a result: (1) measure it in the same metric that type targets — a type = "NNSdep" target with NNS.dep(...)$Dependence (unsigned), a "spearman"/"pearson" target with rank/linear correlation; a signed correlation taken on an unsigned "NNSdep" target is not comparable to ρ\rho and can even read negative while the dependence target is met. (2) The ensemble is the per-observation mean of the replicates — a central summary, not a single series carrying the target dependence — so a rank or linear correlation taken directly on the ensemble tends to read higher than the per-replicate ρ\rho (averaging amplifies the shared order). Calibrate ρ\rho on the replicates, not the ensemble.

target_drift Specification

We can also specify a target drift in our replicates with the target_drift parameter.

boots = NNS.MC(x, reps = 1, lower_rho = -1, upper_rho = 1, by = .5, target_drift = 0.05)$replicates
reps = do.call(cbind, boots)

plot(x, type = "l", lwd = 3, ylim = c(min(c(x, reps)), max(c(x, reps))))
matplot(reps, type = "l", col = rainbow(length(boots)), add = TRUE)

Please see the full NNS.meboot and NNS.MC argument documentation.

Simulating a Multivariate Dependence Structure

A marginal rank transformation can transfer the empirical rank arrangement of continuous observations to chosen new marginal distributions. It does not identify a unique copula when marginals have atoms, and a positive-degree partial-moment transform generally changes the original marginal probability law.

Use degree-zero probabilities for this frequency construction. For these continuous samples, subtracting half an observation from the empirical CDF ranks keeps probability levels away from zero and one. Inverting with degree-zero LPM.VaR applies the target empirical quantile function (type7 interpolation).

set.seed(123)
x <- rnorm(1000); y <- rnorm(1000); z <- rnorm(1000)
original.data <- cbind(x, y, z, x_copy = x)
n <- nrow(original.data)
dep.structure <- apply(original.data, 2, function(v) {
  LPM.ratio(degree = 0, target = v, variable = v) - .5 / n
})
new.data <- replicate(ncol(original.data), rnorm(2000, mean = 10, sd = 20))
new.dep.data <- vapply(seq_len(ncol(original.data)), function(j) {
  LPM.VaR(percentile = dep.structure[, j], degree = 0, x = new.data[, j])
}, numeric(n))

cor(original.data, method = "spearman")
cor(new.dep.data, method = "spearman")

The output has one row per original rank tuple, here 1000, even though the new marginal reference samples have 2000 rows. It approximates those reference marginals at the supplied ranks. For tied marginals, specify a tie policy or randomized probability transform within each CDF jump; ordinary inclusive CDF values are not uniform at atoms. Positive-degree transformations remain useful for directional severity modelling, with their changed target stated explicitly.

Alternative Using NNS.meboot

Alternatively, if we wish to keep the simulated values close to the original data, we can apply the NNS.meboot procedure to each of the variables.

We generate 100 replicates per column at ρ=0.95\rho = 0.95 and compare the column ensembles with the original data.

# Apply bootstrap to each variable
new.boot.dep.data = apply(original.data, 2, function(r) NNS.meboot(r, reps = 100, rho = .95))

# Reformat into vectors
boot.ensemble.vectors = lapply(new.boot.dep.data, function(z) unlist(z["ensemble",]))

# Create matrix from vectors
new.boot.dep.matrix = do.call(cbind, boot.ensemble.vectors)

Checking ensemble correlations with original.data:

for(i in 1:4) print(cor(new.boot.dep.matrix[,i], original.data[,i], method = "spearman"))

#> [1] 0.9885851
#> [1] 0.9965075
#> [1] 0.9906302
#> [1] 0.9901535

Reading these numbers. Here ensemble is the per-observation mean of the replicates, a central summary. Its correlation with the input is not the requested per-replicate target. Alignment is applied to individual residual paths; averaging and trend reconstruction can change the measured correlation. Treat the ensemble as a representative path and inspect achieved correlations for the requested output.

Compare Multivariate Dependence Structures

Column-wise scenario generation does not guarantee preservation of the full joint law or every multivariate dependence statistic. Compare the achieved structure explicitly.

NNS.copula(original.data)
NNS.copula(new.boot.dep.matrix)

#> [1] 0.4452914
#> [1] 0.4423774
head(original.data)
head(new.boot.dep.matrix)

#>                x           y          z      x_copy
